Anne Locke
an lok
n. (Anne Vaughan Locke, c. 1533–c. 1590, English translator and poet)
Hebrew Channah, grace, through Anne; English Locke, from her first husband's family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Anne Locke was a London merchant's daughter who sailed to Geneva in 1557 with two small children, one of whom died within days of arriving, to sit under the preaching of the exiled English church. She translated Calvin's sermons on the thirty-eighth chapter of Isaiah into English and published them in 1560, appending a sequence of sonnets on the fifty-first Psalm, which is the first sonnet sequence in English by anybody. John Knox counted her among the closest of his correspondents and wrote to her with a frankness he showed almost no one else. She later married the Puritan minister Edward Dering and then a preacher of Exeter. Her verse is a woman's confession of sin and plea for mercy set in strict metre, which is what the Psalm she chose actually is (Psa 68:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines translate as to render into another language, and sonnet as a short poem of fourteen lines.

expand to see more

TRANSLA'TE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.

SON'NET, n. A short poem of fourteen lines, two stanzas of four verses each, and two of three each, the rhymes being adjusted by a particular rule.

MED'ITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind.

PEN'ITENT, a. Suffering pain or sorrow of heart on account of sins, crimes or offenses; contrite.

Modern Corruption

Calvin's Isaiah sermons in English, and the first sonnet sequence in the language.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern recovery of Anne Locke purely as a literary first, with the content of what she wrote treated as the period's unavoidable packaging. The content is the thing. She chose the fifty-first Psalm, the confession of a man caught in adultery and murder, and she wrote twenty-six sonnets on it. That is not decoration; it is the doctrine of sin and grace in the hardest form English verse had yet attempted.

The principle to recover is that the word is published by many hands and that translation and sacred verse are among them. “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). The wise woman's mouth is an instrument of instruction in its own sphere: “She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness” (Pro 31:26). And the appointed use of psalms is congregational and mutual: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew basar (H1319), to publish good tidings; Hebrew chokmah (H2451), wisdom, skill.

Hebrew basar (H1319) — to publish, to bear or bring good tidings; Psalm 68:11.

Hebrew tsaba (H6635) — a host, a company, an army; Psalm 68:11.

Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill, sound judgment; Proverbs 31:26.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — kindness, mercy, steadfast love; Proverbs 31:26.

Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to admonish, to warn, to instruct; Colossians 3:16.

Usage

"“great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11) — Geneva, 1557, with two small children."

"“She openeth her mouth with wisdom” (Pro 31:26) — twenty-six sonnets on the fifty-first Psalm."

"“teaching and admonishing one another in psalms” (Col 3:16) — and Knox wrote to her plainly."
